Create vacuum, ensure NO maternal tissue is trapped under the cup, then increase to working pressure.
Apply steady traction in the axis of the pelvis only WITH contractions + maternal effort. Re-assess descent each pull.

steps.step: Abandon if no progress / failure criteria met
steps.detail: Stop + move to caesarean if: no descent with 3 pulls, ≥ 3 cup detachments, or > 15–20 min. Do NOT use sequential instruments.

redFlags: No descent / failure criteria → caesarean (do not persist).
Cup detachments (re-check placement + traction direction).
Suspected fetal scalp trauma.
Shoulder dystocia after head delivery.
postProcedureCare: Neonatal review — observe for cephalhaematoma, subgaleal haemorrhage (can be life-threatening — monitor), jaundice, retinal haemorrhage.
Maternal: examine for tears, estimate blood loss, repair episiotomy.
Document indication, attempts, outcome.

complications.management: Monitor head circumference + signs of shock; neonatal intensive care; transfuse.
Observe; monitor for jaundice.
Repair tears; PPH protocol.

title: Emergency umbilical vein catheterisation (neonatal)
indications: Emergency vascular access in a collapsing / resuscitating newborn (drugs, fluids, glucose) when peripheral access fails.
Exchange transfusion / central access in the first days of life.
equipment: Umbilical catheter (3.5 F preterm / 5 F term).
Umbilical tape, scalpel, forceps, three-way tap, primed with saline.
consentNotes: Emergency — implied consent. Communicate with family + document.

steps.step: Aseptic technique + prime catheter + measure insertion depth
steps.detail: Strict asepsis. Flush the catheter with saline + close the tap (air embolism risk). For EMERGENCY use, insert only ~2–4 cm until blood flows freely (low-lying — avoid liver/portal injury). For indwelling lines, calculate depth + confirm position on X-ray.
Loop umbilical tape at the base for haemostasis. Cut the cord ~1–2 cm from the skin. Identify the single large thin-walled VEIN (vs two thick-walled arteries).
Insert the primed catheter into the vein, advancing gently until free blood return (emergency: just past the abdominal wall). Do not force.
Aspirate to confirm, secure the catheter, give resuscitation drugs / glucose / fluids. Confirm position with X-ray before prolonged use.

redFlags: Inability to aspirate blood (malposition).
Signs of air embolism.
Hepatic injury (catheter in portal system) on X-ray — withdraw.
Infection.
postProcedureCare: Confirm tip position radiographically before non-emergency use.
Monitor for infection, thrombosis, bleeding from the stump.
Remove as soon as alternative access established (infection risk).

complications.management: Always keep the line closed / primed; treat embolism (left lateral head-down, 100% O₂).
Confirm position; use low-lying emergency placement; withdraw if intrahepatic.
Remove line; antibiotics; anticoagulation per neonatology.

references.label: WHO / AAP Neonatal Emergency Vascular Access

title: Suprapubic catheterisation
indications: Acute urinary retention where urethral catheterisation has failed or is contraindicated (e.g. urethral trauma, stricture, false passage).

relative: Previous lower abdominal surgery / adhesions (bowel injury risk).

equipment: Suprapubic catheter kit (Seldinger or trocar) + drainage bag.
Ultrasound (strongly recommended to confirm a full bladder + avoid bowel).
Local anaesthetic + needle, scalpel, antiseptic, sterile drape.
consentNotes: Counsel on indication, bowel injury risk, bleeding, infection, alternatives. Document.

steps.step: Confirm a distended bladder with ultrasound + identify bowel-free track
steps.detail: DO NOT proceed without confirming a full, palpable/sonographically-distended bladder + a clear midline track ~2 cm above the symphysis. Ultrasound markedly reduces bowel injury. Senior / urology if any doubt.
Antiseptic, sterile drape. Infiltrate local anaesthetic in the midline 2 cm above the symphysis, aspirating until urine confirms the track + depth.
Small skin incision. Advance the trocar/Seldinger system perpendicularly (slightly caudal) until urine flows, then advance the catheter + remove the introducer. Inflate the balloon.
Connect drainage, secure the catheter, dress. Drain slowly if grossly distended (avoid decompression haematuria).

redFlags: Bowel content / faeculent aspirate → bowel injury: stop + surgical referral.
Heavy haematuria.
Inability to confirm bladder — abandon.
Decompression haematuria.
postProcedureCare: Monitor output + for haematuria. Drain large volumes gradually.
Catheter care + planned change interval. Urology follow-up for the underlying cause.

complications.management: Ultrasound guidance prevents; surgical management if it occurs.
Irrigation; correct coagulopathy.
Confirm urine flow; reposition / imaging.

title: Intraosseous access (paediatric)
indications: Emergency vascular access in a critically ill / arrested child when peripheral IV access fails within 60–90 sec or 2 attempts.

absolute: Previous IO / orthopaedic hardware in the same bone.

equipment: IO device (drill / manual needle) + appropriate needle size for weight.
Antiseptic, syringe + saline flush, three-way tap.
Lignocaine for the conscious child (intraosseous infusion is painful).
consentNotes: Emergency — implied consent. Inform + reassure family. Document.

steps.step: Select a fracture-free site + confirm landmarks
steps.detail: Preferred: proximal tibia (2–3 cm below + medial to the tibial tuberosity, flat antero-medial surface). Confirm no fracture / prior IO in that bone.
Aseptic prep. Insert the needle perpendicular to the bone using the drill / manual rotation until a 'give' is felt entering the marrow. Remove the stylet.
Needle stands without support; aspirate marrow (may not always); flush with saline freely without extravasation. Give lignocaine slowly before infusion in the conscious child.
Give fluids (often need a pressure bag / push) + any resuscitation drug (same doses as IV). Secure + monitor the site.

redFlags: Extravasation / swelling around the site → remove (risk of compartment syndrome).
Inability to flush.
Signs of compartment syndrome in the limb.
postProcedureCare: Replace with definitive IV / central access as soon as feasible (remove within 24 h).
Monitor the limb for compartment syndrome + infection.
Document insertion time.

complications.management: Remove needle; monitor; fasciotomy if confirmed.
Remove early; antibiotics if infection.
Correct landmarks; avoid the physis.

title: Intra-articular corticosteroid injection
indications: Symptomatic relief of inflammatory / osteoarthritic joint pain after aspiration has excluded sepsis + crystal arthropathy is managed.
Mono/oligo-arthritis flare (e.g. knee OA, gout once infection excluded).

absolute: Septic arthritis / overlying skin infection / bacteraemia.
relative: Recent injection of the same joint (limit frequency).

equipment: Aspiration kit (always aspirate first if effusion / to exclude sepsis).
consentNotes: Counsel on temporary relief, post-injection flare, infection risk (rare), skin/fat atrophy, transient glycaemic rise in diabetics, limit on injection frequency. Document.

steps.step: Exclude joint sepsis + overlying infection BEFORE injecting steroid
steps.detail: If an effusion is present, ASPIRATE first + exclude infection / crystals. NEVER inject steroid into a potentially septic joint (catastrophic). Inspect skin — no overlying infection.
Antiseptic, sterile field + gloves. Identify the safe approach for the joint.
Aspirate any effusion (send for analysis). Without moving the needle (if using one-needle technique) inject the steroid + lignocaine mixture into the joint space — should flow without resistance.
Withdraw, apply dressing, rest the joint briefly.

redFlags: Worsening pain + fever + hot swollen joint after injection → septic arthritis: aspirate + IV antibiotics + orthopaedics.
Injecting against resistance (not intra-articular).
Diabetic hyperglycaemia.
postProcedureCare: Relative rest of the joint 24–48 h.
Warn re post-injection flare (first 24–48 h) + when to seek help (infection).
Diabetics — monitor glucose. Limit repeat injections (e.g. ≤ 3–4/year/joint).

complications.management: Strict asepsis + exclude sepsis first; urgent washout + antibiotics if it occurs.
Reassure; analgesia; ice.
Avoid superficial injection; counsel.

title: Shoulder dystocia management (HELPERR)
indications: Failure of the shoulders to deliver after the fetal head, with gentle axial traction (obstetric emergency — turtle-neck sign).
equipment: Senior obstetrician + neonatal team + anaesthetist (call immediately).
consentNotes: Time-critical emergency — implied consent. Communicate the emergency to the mother + continuous reassurance. Document timeline + manoeuvres.

steps.step: Call for help + STOP routine traction + note the time
steps.detail: Declare shoulder dystocia, summon senior obstetric + neonatal + anaesthetic help, start the clock. AVOID downward traction, fundal pressure, or excessive force (Erb's palsy + fracture risk).
Hyperflex maternal hips onto the abdomen (McRoberts) — resolves ~40 % alone.
Apply suprapubic pressure (downward + lateral, CPR-style) over the fetal anterior shoulder to adduct + dislodge it. Consider episiotomy for access (does not relieve the bony obstruction itself).
Rubin II (push anterior shoulder toward fetal chest) ± Woods screw / reverse Woods to rotate the shoulders to the oblique.
Deliver the posterior arm by sweeping it across the fetal chest (most effective manoeuvre after McRoberts + suprapubic).
Roll the mother onto all-fours (Gaskin). Last resort: cleidotomy, symphysiotomy, or Zavanelli (cephalic replacement + caesarean).

redFlags: Prolonged head-to-body delivery interval (hypoxia risk).
Postpartum haemorrhage + perineal trauma (maternal).
Brachial plexus injury / clavicle or humerus fracture (neonatal).
Failed manoeuvres → senior + last-resort techniques.
postProcedureCare: Neonatal review — Erb's palsy, fracture, hypoxic injury.
Maternal — examine for PPH + third/fourth-degree tear.
Debrief mother + family + team; complete detailed documentation of sequence + timing.
Risk-assessment + counselling for future deliveries.

complications.management: Avoid traction/fundal pressure; physiotherapy; most resolve; refer if persistent.
Prompt delivery; neonatal resuscitation + cooling where indicated.
PPH protocol; trained perineal repair.

references.label: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy + Childbirth

title: Bimanual uterine compression for PPH
indications: Primary postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony — immediate mechanical control while uterotonics + resuscitation are given.
equipment: Concurrent: IV access ×2, uterotonics, blood products, help summoned.
consentNotes: Life-threatening emergency — implied consent. Communicate + reassure. Document.

steps.step: Call for help + activate massive haemorrhage protocol + give uterotonics
steps.detail: Declare PPH, summon senior + anaesthetist + theatre + blood bank. Concurrently: oxytocin → ergometrine → carboprost → tranexamic acid 1 g IV + fluids/blood. Compression buys time, it does not replace these.

steps.step: Rub up a contraction + empty the bladder
steps.detail: Massage the uterine fundus to stimulate contraction; catheterise to empty the bladder (a full bladder impairs contraction).
Insert one hand into the vagina, form a fist in the anterior fornix; place the other hand abdominally behind the uterus; compress the uterus firmly between both hands to tamponade the placental bed.
Maintain compression while uterotonics take effect + resuscitation continues. If bleeding persists → balloon tamponade → surgical (compression sutures, ligation, hysterectomy).

redFlags: Ongoing bleeding despite compression + uterotonics → escalate to balloon / theatre.
Signs of hypovolaemic shock.
Coagulopathy (DIC).
Retained products / trauma / inversion as the cause.
postProcedureCare: Continue monitoring tone + blood loss + vitals.
Continue uterotonic infusion (oxytocin 40 IU over 4 h).
Transfuse + correct coagulopathy. Identify the underlying cause (4 Ts).

complications.management: Massive transfusion + surgical escalation.
Immediate manual replacement; tocolysis; resuscitation.

title: Intrauterine balloon tamponade for PPH
indications: Atonic PPH not controlled by uterotonics + bimanual compression, before / instead of laparotomy — including low-resource condom-catheter tamponade.

absolute: Arterial bleeding needing surgery (e.g. trauma, rupture).

equipment: Bakri balloon OR condom tied to a Foley/uterine catheter (condom-catheter tamponade — WHO-endorsed low-cost option).
Sterile saline 250–500 mL + giving set / syringe.
Vaginal pack to hold the balloon in place.
consentNotes: Emergency — implied consent; counsel where possible. Document insertion + volume + time.

steps.step: Confirm atony is the cause + exclude trauma/rupture/retained products
steps.detail: Tamponade treats ATONIC bleeding. Exclude + treat genital-tract trauma, retained products, and uterine rupture first (these need different management). Empty the bladder.
Under aseptic technique, pass the balloon/condom-catheter through the cervix into the uterine cavity (speculum + sponge forceps help).
Inflate with warm saline (Bakri ~300–500 mL; condom until bleeding stops) until the balloon tamponades the cavity + bleeding slows. Place a vaginal pack to prevent expulsion.
If bleeding stops → tamponade successful; if it continues → proceed to laparotomy. Keep in situ 6–24 h with oxytocin infusion + antibiotics.

redFlags: Continued bleeding after inflation (tamponade-test failure) → laparotomy.
Signs of rupture / concealed bleeding.
Sepsis.
postProcedureCare: Oxytocin infusion + prophylactic antibiotics while balloon in situ.
Monitor blood loss + vitals + urine output.
Plan deflation/removal in 6–24 h in a setting able to manage re-bleed.
Transfuse / correct coagulopathy as needed.

complications.management: Laparotomy — compression sutures, ligation, hysterectomy.
Prophylactic antibiotics; limit dwell time.
Gentle technique; surgical review if suspected.

title: Assisted vaginal breech delivery
indications: Vaginal breech delivery — planned (selected) or unavoidable (advanced labour / second twin / no time for caesarean).

absolute: Footling breech with cord-prolapse risk (usually caesarean).
Hyperextended fetal head, estimated fetal weight discordant, contracted pelvis (favour caesarean where feasible).

consentNotes: Counsel on risks (cord prolapse, head entrapment, hypoxia, trauma) + alternative caesarean. Document.

steps.step: Confirm full dilatation + 'hands-off' until the buttocks deliver spontaneously
steps.detail: Do NOT pull. Allow spontaneous descent to the umbilicus with maternal effort ('hands off the breech'). Premature traction causes nuchal arms + head entrapment.
Allow spontaneous delivery to the scapulae. Keep the fetal back anterior. Use Pinard manoeuvre to flex + deliver the legs if needed.
Rotate the body to deliver each arm anteriorly under the symphysis (Løvset manoeuvre) if the arms do not deliver spontaneously.

Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit (flexion via finger on the maxilla + suprapubic pressure by an assistant) OR forceps to the after-coming head. Keep the head flexed; control delivery to avoid rapid decompression.

redFlags: Cord prolapse.
Head entrapment / hyperextension.
Nuchal arms.
Failure to progress → emergency caesarean if before full descent.
Neonatal hypoxia.
postProcedureCare: Neonatal review — birth trauma + hypoxia.
Maternal — examine for trauma + PPH.
Document manoeuvres + timing. Debrief.

complications.management: MSV / forceps; McRoberts; incise cervix if entrapped at incomplete dilatation; symphysiotomy as last resort.
Expedite delivery; relieve compression.
Gentle technique; neonatal assessment.

references.label: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy + Childbirth

title: Amniotomy (artificial rupture of membranes)
indications: Induction / augmentation of labour with a favourable cervix + engaged head.
To assess liquor (meconium) or apply a fetal scalp electrode.

relative: HIV with high viral load / active genital herpes (consider risks).

consentNotes: Explain purpose, that it commits to delivery, cord-prolapse risk, irreversibility. Document fetal heart before + after.

steps.step: Confirm engaged presenting part + exclude praevia + record FHR before rupture
steps.detail: Vaginal exam: cephalic, engaged, well-applied to the cervix, NO cord felt, exclude vasa/placenta praevia. Record the fetal heart rate immediately before rupture (cord-prolapse + bradycardia risk).
Introduce the amnihook along the examining fingers, rupture the membranes during a contraction with the head applied, controlling the rate of liquor release (especially in polyhydramnios).
Note colour/volume of liquor (meconium?). Feel for cord prolapse. Confirm the presenting part remains applied.
Auscultate / CTG immediately after — a deceleration suggests cord prolapse/compression.

redFlags: Cord felt / prolapse after rupture → obstetric emergency (relieve pressure + immediate delivery).
Fetal bradycardia.
Heavy bleeding (suspect vasa/placenta praevia or abruption).
Meconium-stained liquor.
postProcedureCare: Continue fetal monitoring.
Document time of rupture, liquor, FHR.
Watch for prolonged rupture (infection risk) + cord complications.

complications.management: Relieve presenting-part pressure (knee-chest / fill bladder), tocolysis, immediate delivery (usually caesarean).
Immediate delivery; neonatal resuscitation/transfusion.
Antibiotics; expedite delivery.

title: External cephalic version (ECV)
indications: Breech / transverse presentation at ≥ 36–37 weeks, to enable vaginal cephalic delivery + avoid caesarean.

absolute: Indication for caesarean anyway (e.g. placenta praevia).
Multiple pregnancy (except delivery of second twin).

consentNotes: Counsel on ~50 % success, discomfort, small risk of emergency caesarean (~0.5 %), abruption, transient FHR changes. Document.

steps.step: Confirm eligibility, normal CTG, theatre availability + Rh status
steps.detail: Ultrasound to confirm presentation/placenta/liquor. Reactive CTG before + after. Theatre + emergency caesarean must be available. Check rhesus status (anti-D needed if Rh-negative). Tocolysis improves success.
Give a tocolytic to relax the uterus (improves success, especially in nulliparous women).
Disengage the breech, then apply a 'forward roll' (or back-flip) using both hands to rotate the fetus to cephalic, monitoring maternal comfort. Stop if painful / FHR abnormal / patient declines.
Confirm presentation + reactive CTG afterwards. Give anti-D to Rh-negative women (feto-maternal haemorrhage). Kleihauer if indicated.

redFlags: Fetal bradycardia / abnormal CTG during the procedure → stop + prepare for delivery.
Vaginal bleeding (abruption).
Persistent pain.
Reduced fetal movements after.
postProcedureCare: Monitor CTG until reactive. Anti-D for Rh-negative.
Advise to report bleeding / pain / reduced movements.
Plan mode of delivery based on the outcome.

complications.management: Immediate delivery; resuscitation.
Stop; reposition; deliver if persistent.
Anti-D; Kleihauer; monitor.

title: Symphysiotomy (last-resort obstructed labour)
indications: Obstructed labour / trapped after-coming head in breech / shoulder dystocia, where caesarean is NOT available + the fetus is alive — a last-resort, life-saving procedure in low-resource settings.

absolute: Dead fetus where destructive delivery is more appropriate.
Non-engaged head / gross disproportion where delivery still impossible.

equipment: Two assistants to support the legs.
consentNotes: Last-resort emergency. Counsel on long-term pelvic pain / instability / incontinence risks vs life-saving necessity. Document fully.

steps.step: Confirm no caesarean option + live fetus + head ≥ 3/5 engaged + bladder catheterised + abduction limited
steps.detail: Symphysiotomy is ONLY justified when caesarean is unavailable + delivery is otherwise impossible. Catheterise + displace the urethra laterally with a sound (protect it). Limit leg abduction to < 90° (over-abduction tears the SI joints + urethra).
Local anaesthetic over the symphysis. Two assistants support + moderately abduct the thighs (≤ 90°). Insert a metal catheter to push the urethra to one side.
With a scalpel/sound, divide the cartilage of the symphysis pubis in the midline (partial — ~1–2 cm separation), keeping clear of the displaced urethra.
Deliver promptly (often with vacuum/assisted technique). Then close the skin, leave a catheter in situ several days, strap the pelvis.

redFlags: Urethral / bladder injury.
Excessive separation / SI joint disruption.
Haemorrhage.
Long-term pelvic instability / pain / incontinence / fistula.
postProcedureCare: Indwelling urinary catheter 5–7 days.
Pelvic strapping / bed rest, then graded mobilisation.
Antibiotics + analgesia.
Counsel + follow-up for incontinence + pelvic pain; family planning + future delivery planning.

complications.management: Prolonged catheter; fistula repair referral.
Physiotherapy; strapping; analgesia.
Antibiotics; haemostasis.

references.label: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy + Childbirth (Symphysiotomy)

title: Lateral canthotomy + cantholysis (orbital compartment syndrome)
indications: Sight-threatening orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar haemorrhage (trauma / post-surgical) — acute proptosis + raised IOP + reduced vision/RAPD. SIGHT-SAVING + TIME-CRITICAL.

absolute: Suspected globe rupture (do NOT decompress — worsens extrusion).

consentNotes: Sight-saving emergency — implied consent. Inform patient/family + ophthalmology urgently. Document vision/IOP.

steps.step: Confirm orbital compartment syndrome + exclude globe rupture
steps.detail: Diagnose clinically: acute proptosis, very high IOP (> 40), reduced acuity / RAPD, 'rock-hard' eye — do NOT wait for imaging if vision is threatened. EXCLUDE globe rupture first (canthotomy contraindicated in rupture).
Inject local anaesthetic with adrenaline into the lateral canthus. Clamp the lateral canthus with a haemostat for ~1 min (haemostasis + crush).
Cut the crushed lateral canthus horizontally ~1 cm down to the orbital rim with scissors.

Pull the lower lid outward, strum + cut the INFERIOR limb of the lateral canthal tendon (point scissors toward the patient's nose/chin). The lid should become free + mobile — this is what relieves the pressure. Re-check IOP/vision.

redFlags: Suspected globe rupture (do not perform).
Persistent high IOP after cantholysis (incomplete — release the tendon fully).
Ongoing haemorrhage.
postProcedureCare: Urgent ophthalmology.
Re-check IOP + vision. Manage the underlying haemorrhage + raised IOP (acetazolamide, mannitol).
The canthus is repaired later by ophthalmology/plastics.

complications.management: Decompress within ~60–120 min of vision loss; complete cantholysis.
Exclude rupture before procedure; ophthalmology.
Haemostasis; later canthal repair.

title: Escharotomy (circumferential full-thickness burn)
indications: Circumferential full-thickness burn causing limb compartment compromise (loss of pulses, ↑ compartment pressure) or chest-wall restriction impairing ventilation. LIMB/LIFE-SAVING.
equipment: Analgesia / sedation (full-thickness eschar is insensate but edges + deeper tissue are not).
consentNotes: Emergency — implied consent. Discuss with burns/surgical team. Document neurovascular + ventilation status.

steps.step: Confirm true circumferential full-thickness burn with distal compromise / ventilatory restriction
steps.detail: Indicated for circumferential full-thickness burns with: absent distal pulses / rising compartment pressure / cold cyanotic limb, OR chest-wall restriction with rising airway pressures. Mark the planned mid-axial incision lines, avoiding key nerves/vessels.

Incise through the full thickness of the burnt eschar (NOT into deep fascia — that is fasciotomy) along the mid-medial + mid-lateral lines of the limb; the eschar should spring open. For the chest, incise the anterior axillary lines + a transverse subcostal line.
Distal perfusion returns (Doppler/pulses) / ventilation improves. Extend the incision until release is achieved, crossing involved joints.
Achieve haemostasis (cautery), apply burns dressings, reassess perfusion + ventilation.

redFlags: Persistent ischaemia after escharotomy → consider compartment syndrome needing fasciotomy.
Significant bleeding from incisions.
Inadequate release / ongoing ventilatory compromise.
postProcedureCare: Transfer to a burns centre.
Reassess perfusion + ventilation frequently.
Fluid resuscitation (Parkland), analgesia, tetanus, infection prevention.
Wound care + later grafting.

complications.management: Extend incisions; consider fasciotomy.
Cautery; antibiotics; dressings.
Follow correct mid-axial lines.

title: Manual reduction of paraphimosis
indications: Paraphimosis — a retracted foreskin trapped behind the glans causing oedema + venous congestion (urological emergency; ischaemia risk if delayed).

relative: Inability to tolerate without sedation (consider analgesia/block).

equipment: Granulated sugar / ice glove / compression wrap (osmotic + oedema-reduction adjuncts).
Fine needle (for puncture technique if needed).
consentNotes: Explain the emergency, manoeuvre, analgesia, small risk of needing a dorsal slit. Document.

steps.step: Confirm paraphimosis + assess glans viability + provide analgesia first
steps.detail: Confirm the constricting band behind the glans + assess for ischaemia/necrosis. Provide adequate analgesia ± penile block — reduction is painful + impossible if the patient guards. Necrotic glans → urgent urology.
Reduce glans oedema first: sustained manual compression (5–15 min) ± osmotic agents (granulated sugar, 50% dextrose-soaked gauze) ± ice/cold to shrink the glans.
Place both thumbs on the glans + fingers behind the constricting band; apply steady pressure to push the glans back through the band while drawing the foreskin forward.
Confirm the foreskin is back in the normal position + circulation restored. If reduction fails → urgent urology for dorsal slit / emergency circumcision.

redFlags: Glans ischaemia / necrosis.
Failed reduction → urology for dorsal slit.
Recurrent paraphimosis (elective circumcision).
postProcedureCare: Advise to always reduce the foreskin after retraction (catheter care!).
Analgesia; monitor for recurrence.
Refer for elective circumcision if recurrent / phimotic.

complications.management: Time-critical reduction; urology; possible debridement.
Dorsal slit / emergency circumcision by urology.

title: Manual detorsion of testicular torsion
indications: Suspected testicular torsion when definitive surgical exploration will be delayed — a temporising manoeuvre that does NOT replace emergency scrotal exploration.

relative: Should never delay surgery — exploration + fixation is definitive.

equipment: Doppler ultrasound (if immediately available — must not delay surgery).
consentNotes: Explain the emergency, that surgery is still required, and the temporising aim. Document time of onset (salvage is time-critical).

steps.step: Recognise torsion + call urology for emergency exploration FIRST
steps.detail: Sudden severe testicular pain + high-riding/horizontal testis + absent cremasteric reflex = torsion until proven otherwise. Surgical exploration within 6 h gives ~100 % salvage. Manual detorsion is only a bridge — arrange theatre immediately + do NOT delay for imaging.
Provide analgesia ± spermatic cord block to allow the manoeuvre.

Most torsions twist medially/inward → rotate the testis OUTWARD (lateral), like opening a book (patient's right testis anticlockwise, left clockwise), usually 1–3 turns (360°–720°). Pain relief + lower-lying testis suggest success.
If pain worsens, try rotating the other direction. Whether or not detorsion succeeds, the patient STILL needs emergency exploration + bilateral orchidopexy.

redFlags: Worsening pain on detorsion (wrong direction / incomplete).
Time from onset > 6 h (falling salvage).
Do NOT let manual detorsion delay surgery.
postProcedureCare: Emergency scrotal exploration + bilateral orchidopexy regardless of detorsion outcome.
Document onset + intervention times.
If non-viable → orchidectomy + contralateral fixation.

complications.management: Emergency exploration; orchidectomy if non-viable; fix contralateral.
Surgery is definitive regardless.

title: Diagnostic ascitic tap (paracentesis for SBP)
indications: Diagnostic sampling of ascites in any cirrhotic patient admitted or clinically deteriorating — to diagnose spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (neutrophils > 250/mm³).

absolute: No safe window (adhesions / distended bowel / surgical scars overlying).
relative: Severe uncorrected coagulopathy / DIC (diagnostic tap usually still safe — do not routinely transfuse first).

equipment: Ultrasound (recommended to mark a safe pocket + avoid bowel/vessels).
Specimen tubes: cell count (EDTA), culture (inoculate blood-culture bottles at the bedside — higher yield), biochemistry (albumin, protein), cytology.
consentNotes: Explain indication, minimal risk (bleeding/infection/bowel injury), benefit of early SBP diagnosis. Document.

steps.step: Identify a safe pocket (ultrasound) avoiding bowel, bladder + epigastric vessels
steps.detail: Use the left lower quadrant (lateral to the rectus, ~2 finger-breadths supero-medial to the ASIS) or an ultrasound-marked pocket. Avoid the rectus sheath (inferior epigastric vessels), scars, distended bladder + visible vessels. Empty the bladder.
Antiseptic, sterile field. Local anaesthetic for larger-bore/therapeutic taps (a diagnostic 21 G needle often needs none).
Insert using a Z-track, aspirate 20–30 mL of ascitic fluid. Inoculate blood-culture bottles at the bedside + send cell count + albumin + protein ± cytology.
Neutrophils > 250/mm³ → start empirical SBP antibiotics (cefotaxime) immediately + IV albumin per protocol. Calculate SAAG (serum-ascites albumin gradient) for the cause of ascites.

redFlags: Aspiration of bowel content (faeculent) → bowel injury: surgical referral.
Persistent bleeding (rare — inferior epigastric injury).
Neutrophils > 250 → treat SBP urgently.
postProcedureCare: Small dressing.
Chase microscopy + culture. Start SBP treatment + albumin if neutrophils > 250 (don't wait for culture).
For large-volume therapeutic taps: albumin replacement 6–8 g per litre removed.

complications.management: Ultrasound guidance prevents; surgical management if it occurs.
Pressure; avoid the rectus sheath.
Z-track technique; stoma bag / suture if needed.

title: Rapid sequence induction + intubation (RSI)
indications: Emergency airway protection / control in a patient at risk of aspiration with a full stomach — reduced GCS, airway compromise, respiratory failure, agitation needing control for imaging/transfer.

absolute: Total upper-airway obstruction where intubation will fail + no surgical-airway backup.
relative: Anticipated difficult airway (plan + senior + awake technique).

equipment: Laryngoscope (+ video laryngoscope), ETTs (sized + 1 above/below), bougie, stylet.
Induction agent (ketamine / etomidate / propofol) + paralytic (rocuronium / suxamethonium) + push-dose vasopressor.
Monitoring (ECG, SpO₂, BP, ETCO₂) + IV access ×2.
consentNotes: Emergency — implied consent. Brief the team, assign roles, verbalise the plan + failed-airway plan. Document.

steps.step: Prepare + pre-oxygenate + plan for failure (the 7 Ps)
steps.detail: Preparation, Pre-oxygenation (3 min / 8 vital-capacity breaths, apnoeic O₂), Pretreatment, Paralysis+induction, Positioning, Placement+proof, Post-intubation care. Check equipment, assign roles, prepare a failed-airway plan + surgical-airway backup BEFORE giving drugs.
Resuscitate first where possible (fluids/blood/vasopressor) — 'resuscitate before you intubate'. Position (ear-to-sternal-notch / ramp).

Give induction agent + rapid-onset paralytic together (e.g. ketamine 1–2 mg/kg + rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg, or suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg). Apply gentle cricoid only if it does not impair the view. Do not bag unless desaturating.
Laryngoscopy + pass the tube. CONFIRM placement with continuous waveform capnography (gold standard) + chest rise + auscultation. Secure the tube + note depth.
Sedation + analgesia infusion, ventilator settings (lung-protective), NG tube, re-check vitals, CXR for tube position, ongoing monitoring.

redFlags: Can't intubate, can't oxygenate → declare failed airway: supraglottic airway → front-of-neck access (cricothyroidotomy).
Peri-induction hypotension/arrest (vasopressor ready).
Oesophageal intubation (capnography catches it).
Desaturation during attempt — stop + re-oxygenate.
postProcedureCare: Maintain sedation + analgesia.
Confirm tube position (capnography + CXR). Secure tube + document depth.
Lung-protective ventilation; monitor; arrange definitive care/transfer.

complications.management: Vortex / DAS failed-airway drill → SGA → front-of-neck access.
Suction; lung-protective ventilation; antibiotics if pneumonitis.
Optimise pre-RSI; push-dose vasopressor; fluids/blood.

title: Spinal (subarachnoid) anaesthesia
indications: Anaesthesia for lower-abdominal / pelvic / lower-limb surgery + caesarean section — the workhorse regional technique, especially in low-resource settings.

absolute: Local infection at the puncture site / systemic sepsis.
relative: Fixed cardiac output states (severe aortic/mitral stenosis).

equipment: IV access + fluid co-load, vasopressor (phenylephrine / ephedrine), full monitoring + resuscitation/airway equipment.
consentNotes: Counsel on technique, hypotension, post-dural-puncture headache, failure, rare serious risks (nerve injury, haematoma, infection, high/total spinal). Document.

steps.step: Confirm fasting, IV access, monitoring, vasopressor + resuscitation ready
steps.detail: Check coagulation, no contraindication, IV access + co-load, BP/ECG/SpO₂ monitoring, vasopressor drawn up, airway + resuscitation equipment immediately available (a high/total spinal can cause apnoea + collapse).
Sitting or lateral, spine flexed. Strict asepsis (mask, sterile gloves, antiseptic, drape). Identify the L3/4 or L4/5 interspace (below the conus, ~L1).
Local anaesthetic to skin. Advance the spinal needle midline through the ligaments until a 'give' (dura) + free flow of clear CSF confirms the subarachnoid space.

Inject the calculated dose of hyperbaric bupivacaine slowly. Position the patient to control spread (baricity + table tilt). Monitor block height + BP closely; treat hypotension promptly with vasopressor + fluids.

redFlags: High/total spinal (rising block, dyspnoea, hypotension, bradycardia, apnoea) → support airway/ventilation + vasopressors + fluids.
Profound hypotension/bradycardia.
Bloody tap / paraesthesia (reposition).
Failed block (alternative anaesthesia).
postProcedureCare: Monitor BP/HR + block regression + return of motor/sensory function + urinary retention.
Manage hypotension. Watch for post-dural-puncture headache (offer fluids/analgesia, blood patch if severe).
Do not discharge until block has regressed + the patient can void + mobilise safely.

complications.management: Airway support + ventilation + vasopressors + fluids until block regresses.
Vasopressor (phenylephrine; ephedrine if bradycardic), fluids, atropine.
Fine pencil-point needle reduces risk; conservative; epidural blood patch if severe.
Avoid in coagulopathy/infection; urgent MRI + neurosurgery if neuro deficit.

references.label: WFSA Spinal Anaesthesia / WHO Surgical Care at the District Hospital

title: Procedural sedation + analgesia
indications: Sedation/analgesia for a painful/distressing procedure (fracture/dislocation reduction, cardioversion, abscess drainage, paediatric imaging).

relative: Recent food (balance urgency vs aspiration risk).

equipment: Oxygen + suction + bag-valve-mask + airway adjuncts + intubation backup.
Sedation agent (ketamine / propofol / midazolam ± opioid) + IV access.
A dedicated clinician for sedation separate from the proceduralist.
consentNotes: Counsel on sedation level, risks (respiratory depression, aspiration, hypotension), fasting status, recovery. Document.

steps.step: Pre-sedation assessment + a dedicated sedation clinician + full monitoring
steps.detail: Assess airway (Mallampati, mouth opening), ASA grade, fasting, comorbidities, allergies. A clinician whose ONLY job is the sedation/airway (separate from the proceduralist) + full monitoring + resuscitation equipment + reversal agents must be ready before starting.
Apply oxygen + capnography. Titrate the agent to the minimum effective sedation depth (e.g. ketamine for dissociative sedation in children; propofol for short procedures with airway skills).
Continuous SpO₂ + ETCO₂ + ECG + BP. Watch for apnoea/obstruction (capnography detects hypoventilation before desaturation). Support the airway as needed.
Recover in a monitored area until awake, protecting airway, vitals stable, pain controlled. Apply formal discharge criteria + responsible escort + written advice.

redFlags: Apnoea / airway obstruction / desaturation → stimulate, airway manoeuvres, BVM, reversal, escalate.
Hypotension.
Laryngospasm (esp. ketamine in children) — positive pressure ± paralysis.
Aspiration.
postProcedureCare: Monitored recovery until discharge criteria met.
Written safety-net + responsible adult escort (no driving/operating machinery 24 h).
Document agents, doses, monitoring, recovery.

complications.management: Airway support, BVM, reversal (naloxone/flumazenil), escalate.
Positive-pressure ventilation; deepen/paralyse if needed.
Suction, lung-protective support, observe.

references.label: RCEM Safe Sedation in the ED

title: Fascia iliaca compartment block
indications: Analgesia for a fractured neck of femur / femoral shaft — reduces opioid use, especially in the elderly.
equipment: Long-acting local anaesthetic (e.g. levobupivacaine / bupivacaine) — calculate max weight-based dose.
Antiseptic, sterile gloves, monitoring + Intralipid available (LAST).
consentNotes: Explain analgesic aim, transient leg weakness/numbness, small risks (bleeding, infection, LA toxicity). Document.

steps.step: Calculate the max safe LA dose + confirm no vascular puncture + Intralipid available
steps.detail: Calculate weight-based maximum local-anaesthetic dose to avoid systemic toxicity (LAST). Confirm monitoring + Intralipid 20% immediately available. Identify the femoral artery + avoid it (block site is lateral to the artery).

Landmark: 1 cm below the junction of the lateral + middle thirds of a line from the ASIS to the pubic tubercle, lateral to the femoral artery. Ultrasound: identify fascia iliaca over iliacus, lateral to the femoral vessels.

steps.step: Inject in the fascia iliaca plane
steps.detail: Advance the needle through fascia lata + fascia iliaca (two 'pops' on landmark technique). Aspirate (no blood), then inject a large volume of dilute LA in the plane, watching it spread under ultrasound.
Confirm improving pain over 20–30 min. Document block + monitor for LA toxicity.

redFlags: LAST — perioral tingling, metallic taste, agitation, seizures, arrhythmia → stop + Intralipid + ALS.
Intravascular injection (aspirate first).
Femoral nerve/vessel injury.
postProcedureCare: Monitor for LA toxicity ~30 min.
Document onset of analgesia; reduce systemic opioids accordingly.
Falls precautions (leg weakness). Re-block / top-up as needed pre-operatively.

complications.management: Stop injection; Intralipid 20% 1.5 mL/kg bolus + infusion; ALS.
Pressure; avoid the femoral artery; ultrasound guidance.
Avoid intraneural injection; usually transient.

references.label: AAGBI Regional Anaesthesia + Fascia Iliaca Block

title: Emergency pericardiocentesis (cardiac tamponade)
indications: Life-threatening cardiac tamponade with haemodynamic compromise (Beck triad, pulsus paradoxus, echo signs) — temporising/life-saving drainage.

absolute: Type A aortic dissection with haemopericardium (pericardiocentesis can worsen — needs surgery; drain only minimal to bridge to theatre).
Traumatic tamponade where thoracotomy is indicated + available.

equipment: Ultrasound / echo (strongly recommended — markedly improves safety).
Long 18 G needle / pericardiocentesis kit + guidewire + pigtail catheter (Seldinger).
consentNotes: Emergency — implied consent. Inform if conscious. Document echo findings + drainage.

steps.step: Confirm tamponade physiology + use ultrasound guidance + exclude dissection
steps.detail: Confirm a significant effusion with tamponade (RA/RV diastolic collapse, dilated IVC, hypotension). USE ULTRASOUND GUIDANCE where available (blind subxiphoid is a last resort). Consider aortic dissection (would need cardiothoracic surgery, not large-volume drainage).
Patient ~30–45° head-up. Antiseptic, sterile drape, local anaesthetic. Choose the ultrasound-identified shortest safe window (often apical/parasternal) or subxiphoid.

steps.step: Insert needle aiming toward the left shoulder, aspirating
steps.detail: Advance under continuous ultrasound (agitated-saline confirmation) aspirating continuously. Subxiphoid: aim toward the left shoulder, just under the costal margin. Stop when fluid is aspirated + haemodynamics improve.
Pass a guidewire, then a pigtail catheter for controlled drainage. Aspirate enough to relieve tamponade; secure the catheter for ongoing drainage. Re-image.

redFlags: Aspirated blood that clots → likely ventricular puncture (pericardial blood is usually defibrinated + does not clot).
New arrhythmia / ST changes (myocardial contact — withdraw).
Rapid re-accumulation (surgical cause).
Pneumothorax.
postProcedureCare: Continuous monitoring + repeat echo for re-accumulation.
Secure the drain; record output.
Treat the underlying cause (malignancy, infection, uraemia, trauma → surgery). Cardiology/cardiothoracic referral.

complications.management: Ultrasound guidance prevents; cardiothoracic surgery if it occurs.
Needle decompression / chest drain.
Withdraw needle from the myocardium; treat rhythm.

title: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) aspiration / incision
indications: Peritonsillar abscess — unilateral severe sore throat, trismus, 'hot potato' voice, uvular deviation, fluctuant peritonsillar swelling.

absolute: Inability to open the mouth adequately (trismus) — ENT.
relative: Young / uncooperative child (often needs ENT under GA).

equipment: Good headlight + tongue depressor + suction (essential — risk of aspiration of pus/blood).
Large-bore needle + syringe (aspiration) or guarded scalpel (incision).
consentNotes: Explain procedure, that it is uncomfortable, risk of bleeding/aspiration, possible recurrence, alternative ENT drainage under GA. Document.

steps.step: Assess + protect the airway + ensure suction is ready
steps.detail: Exclude airway compromise + epiglottitis. Suction MUST be immediately ready (pus/blood aspiration risk). If significant trismus / airway risk / child → ENT (often GA). Beware the medially-placed carotid (aspirate, don't plunge a blade deep/lateral).
Topical anaesthetic spray to the soft palate ± local anaesthetic infiltration at the aspiration site.
Aspirate the point of maximal fluctuance (usually superior pole) with a needle guarded to a safe depth (~1 cm) directed sagittally — NOT laterally (carotid). Aspiration of pus confirms + treats.
If aspiration yields pus but symptoms persist, a small incision + blunt spreading with forceps may be done by an experienced clinician. Give IV antibiotics + steroids + analgesia + fluids.

redFlags: Airway compromise / stridor / drooling → secure airway + ENT urgently.
Brisk bleeding (carotid proximity).
Spread → parapharyngeal / retropharyngeal abscess / mediastinitis / Lemierre's.
Failure to improve → ENT + imaging.
postProcedureCare: IV antibiotics (covering streptococci + anaerobes, e.g. benzylpenicillin + metronidazole / co-amoxiclav) + analgesia + fluids + steroids.
Observe; ENT review. Re-aspirate if re-accumulates.
Tonsillectomy considered for recurrent quinsy.

complications.management: Aspirate at safe depth, sagittal direction; ENT/surgical control if injured.
Continuous suction; sit patient up; airway support.
Imaging + IV antibiotics + surgical drainage.

title: Nasal foreign body removal
indications: Nasal foreign body (common in young children) — unilateral discharge / obstruction / visible object.

absolute: Posterior / impacted FB risking airway, or button battery beyond easy reach → urgent ENT.

equipment: Instruments: blunt hook, crocodile/Tilley forceps, balloon catheter.
consentNotes: Explain technique(s), including the 'parent's kiss', need for ENT if unsuccessful. Reassure child + parent. Document.

steps.step: Identify the FB type — button battery / magnet = emergency removal
steps.detail: Inspect with a headlight. A BUTTON BATTERY or paired MAGNETS causes rapid tissue necrosis/septal perforation → urgent removal/ENT, do not delay. Confirm it is a nasal (not inhaled) FB + the airway is safe.
Position the child on a parent's lap, decongest ± anaesthetise the nostril. Calm, single attempt — repeated attempts push it back + cause oedema.

steps.step: Attempt 'positive pressure' first for soft round objects
steps.detail: 'Parent's kiss' / Beamsley blaster: occlude the unaffected nostril, deliver a puff of positive pressure via the mouth to expel the FB. Atraumatic + often successful.
Direct removal under vision: blunt hook behind a graspable object, or forceps for a graspable FB, or pass a balloon catheter beyond + inflate + withdraw. Refer to ENT if not removed in 1–2 attempts.

redFlags: Button battery / magnets (necrosis) — urgent.
Suspected aspiration (coughing/choking) — treat as airway FB.
Bleeding / posterior displacement.
Failed attempts → ENT (oedema makes it harder).
postProcedureCare: Examine the nostril for residual FB / mucosal injury / battery burn.
Examine the other nostril + ears (children hide multiple FBs).
Safety advice to parents. ENT follow-up if battery injury / septal damage.

complications.management: Emergency removal; ENT; monitor for perforation.
Avoid blind blunt pushing; manage as airway FB if aspirated.
Decongestant; pressure; ENT if persistent.

title: Suprapubic aspiration of urine (infant)
indications: Obtaining an uncontaminated urine sample in an unwell infant (< 2 yrs, especially neonates) when a clean catch fails + UTI must be diagnosed/excluded reliably.

absolute: Empty bladder (no target — confirm fullness first).
Abdominal distension / organomegaly obscuring the bladder.

equipment: Ultrasound (strongly recommended — confirms a full bladder + raises success markedly).
consentNotes: Explain to parents — minimally invasive, transient discomfort, small risk of bleeding/bowel injury, gold-standard sterile sample. Document.

steps.step: Confirm a full bladder with ultrasound + ensure the infant has not recently voided
steps.detail: Ultrasound-confirm urine in the bladder (don't proceed if empty). Ideally aspirate ~30–60 min after a feed/void. A full bladder + ultrasound dramatically improves success + safety.
Supine, legs held (frog-leg). An assistant occludes the urethra (gentle penile/perineal pressure) to prevent voiding. Antiseptic to the suprapubic skin.

steps.step: Aspirate in the midline ~1–2 cm above the symphysis
steps.detail: Insert the needle perpendicular (slightly caudad) in the midline 1–2 cm above the pubic symphysis, aspirating gently as you advance until urine returns. Do not advance further once urine is obtained.
Withdraw, apply brief pressure, dress. Send urine for microscopy + culture (any growth from an SPA sample is significant).

redFlags: Aspiration of bowel content (rare) → observe; surgical review if symptomatic.
Frank haematuria.
Inability to obtain urine (re-attempt later with a fuller bladder).
postProcedureCare: Brief observation. Reassure parents.
Start empirical antibiotics if the unwell infant is septic (don't wait for culture).
Follow up culture; image the urinary tract per UTI guidelines if confirmed.

complications.management: Self-limiting; reassure.
Rare with ultrasound; observe; surgical review if peritonism.

title: Neonatal exchange transfusion
indications: Severe neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia at exchange-threshold (kernicterus risk), severe haemolytic disease of the newborn (rhesus/ABO), or severe anaemia/polycythaemia per protocol.

absolute: Haemodynamically unstable infant not yet resuscitated.

equipment: Umbilical venous catheter (or central access) + three-way taps.
Cross-matched, irradiated, CMV-negative, fresh (< 5 days) reconstituted blood, warmed.
Monitoring (ECG, SpO₂, temperature, glucose), resuscitation equipment.
consentNotes: Counsel parents on indication, isovolumetric technique, risks (electrolyte shifts, NEC, infection, thrombocytopenia, cardiovascular instability). Document.

steps.step: Confirm exchange threshold, correct blood product (cross-matched/irradiated/warmed) + double-isovolumetric plan
steps.detail: Verify bilirubin is at the exchange line on the gestation/age nomogram. CHECK the blood product: correct group, cross-matched, irradiated, CMV-negative, fresh, warmed. Plan a double-volume (~160–180 mL/kg) exchange in small aliquots. Two clinicians check the blood.
Place/confirm umbilical venous (± arterial) access. Send baseline bilirubin, FBC, electrolytes, calcium, glucose, blood gas, group + cross-match.

Remove + replace blood in small aliquots (~5 mL/kg) isovolumetrically over ~1.5–2 h. Continuous monitoring; give calcium gluconate as needed (citrate binds calcium → hypocalcaemia); watch glucose + temperature.
Repeat bilirubin + electrolytes + calcium + glucose + FBC. Continue intensive phototherapy. Watch for rebound hyperbilirubinaemia + complications.

redFlags: Cardiovascular instability / arrhythmia (hyperkalaemia / hypocalcaemia / volume shifts).
Hypoglycaemia (rebound after the glucose load in donor blood).
Necrotising enterocolitis.
Catheter complications / air embolism / infection.
postProcedureCare: Continue intensive phototherapy + monitor for rebound bilirubin.
Monitor electrolytes/calcium/glucose/FBC + for NEC + sepsis.
Neonatology care; investigate + treat the underlying cause (haemolysis).

complications.management: Use fresh blood; give calcium; monitor ECG + treat.
Withhold feeds during; monitor; treat NEC.
Aseptic technique; keep line primed/closed; antibiotics.

title: Manual reduction of an incarcerated inguinal hernia
indications: Incarcerated (irreducible but non-strangulated) inguinal hernia — attempt gentle reduction to convert to a semi-elective repair (especially in infants).

absolute: Signs of strangulation (erythema, severe tenderness, systemic toxicity, peritonism) → emergency surgery, do NOT reduce.

consentNotes: Explain the attempt, that surgery is needed if it fails or strangulation is suspected, risks of reduction. Document duration of incarceration + bowel signs.

steps.detail: Do NOT reduce a strangulated hernia (skin erythema, exquisite tenderness, systemic upset, peritonism, raised lactate) — this needs emergency surgery + reduction could return dead bowel to the abdomen. Assess viability + bowel-obstruction signs.
Provide analgesia ± light sedation. Place head-down (Trendelenburg). An ice pack + waiting reduces oedema + may allow spontaneous reduction (especially infants).
Apply steady, gentle, sustained pressure directing the hernia contents back along the inguinal canal (guide the neck with one hand, milk the contents with the other). Avoid forceful pushing.
Confirm reduction (lump gone, comfort). Admit/observe for a period (delayed strangulation / reduction en masse). Arrange semi-elective repair (urgent in infants — high re-incarceration risk).

redFlags: Any sign of strangulation → emergency theatre, do not reduce.
Reduction 'en masse' (reduces the sac + contents together but obstruction persists).
Ongoing pain / obstruction after apparent reduction.
Infants — high recurrence; expedite repair.
postProcedureCare: Observe after reduction (delayed compromise).
Arrange repair — urgent in infants, semi-elective in adults.
Safety-net: return if pain/vomiting/irreducible lump recurs.

complications.management: Never reduce strangulation; if suspected after reduction → laparotomy.
Recognise persistent obstruction; surgical exploration.
Expedite definitive repair.

title: Reduction of pulled elbow (radial head subluxation)
indications: Pulled elbow (nursemaid's elbow) in a young child — typical history of a sudden axial pull on the arm, child holds the arm pronated + refuses to use it, no swelling/deformity.

absolute: Swelling / deformity / focal bony tenderness / point tenderness over a bone → suspect fracture, get X-ray, do NOT manipulate.
relative: Atypical history / age outside the usual range — image first.

equipment: None essential (no X-ray needed if classic history + exam).
consentNotes: Explain the simple manoeuvre to parents, that it is briefly uncomfortable, common + benign. Document mechanism + exam.

steps.step: Confirm a typical pulled elbow + exclude fracture (no swelling/deformity/bony tenderness)
steps.detail: Classic: axial traction mechanism, arm held pronated + slightly flexed, no swelling, no deformity, no focal bony tenderness. If ANY of those features suggest fracture → X-ray first, do not manipulate.
Support the elbow with one hand (thumb over the radial head), with the other hand fully hyperpronate the forearm. A click is often felt over the radial head.
If hyperpronation fails: supinate the forearm fully then flex the elbow to the shoulder; feel for the click.
The child usually starts using the arm normally within 5–30 min. If they do not, reassess + consider X-ray (alternative diagnosis / fracture).

redFlags: Swelling/deformity/bony tenderness → fracture: X-ray, do not manipulate.
Failure to use the arm after successful-feeling reduction → reassess + image.
Recurrent episodes (advise parents to avoid pulling).
postProcedureCare: No immobilisation needed once using the arm.
Reassure parents; advise against lifting/pulling the child by the hands/wrists.
Safety-net: return if not using the arm / swelling appears.

complications.management: Image if atypical / swelling / failure to recover.
Parental advice; usually outgrows by age 5–6.

title: Intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier's block)
indications: Anaesthesia of a forearm/hand for a short procedure (e.g. Colles fracture reduction, minor surgery) lasting < 60 min.

absolute: Use of bupivacaine for IVRA (cardiotoxic on tourniquet release — NEVER).
Inability to apply/maintain a reliable tourniquet.
Severe peripheral vascular disease / sickle cell / Raynaud's (relative-absolute).

equipment: Two IV cannulae (one in the operative limb distally, one in the other arm).
Esmarch bandage, full monitoring, Intralipid + resuscitation equipment.
consentNotes: Explain the tourniquet discomfort, numbness, the critical need to keep the cuff inflated, LA toxicity risk. Document.

steps.step: Confirm a tested double-cuff tourniquet + use prilocaine (never bupivacaine) + Intralipid ready
steps.detail: Verify the pneumatic tourniquet holds pressure reliably (the entire safety of the technique depends on it). Use prilocaine, NEVER bupivacaine (cardiac arrest on release). Monitoring + Intralipid + resuscitation equipment must be ready. Confirm cuff inflation time will be ≥ 20 min before any deflation.

Insert a distal IV cannula in the operative limb + one in the other arm. Elevate + exsanguinate with an Esmarch bandage, then inflate the proximal cuff to ~100 mmHg above systolic. Confirm the limb is pulseless.

Inject prilocaine slowly through the operative-limb cannula (weight-based dose). Anaesthesia develops within ~10 min. Switch to the distal cuff over the anaesthetised area if tourniquet pain develops.

steps.step: Maintain the cuff ≥ 20 min, then deflate in cycles
steps.detail: NEVER deflate the cuff within 20 min of injection (bolus LA release). At the end, deflate in short cycles (deflate–reinflate) while watching for LA toxicity.

redFlags: Early/accidental cuff deflation → bolus LA toxicity (seizures, arrhythmia) → Intralipid + ALS.
Tourniquet failure mid-procedure.
Tourniquet pain → use distal cuff.
Signs of LAST.
postProcedureCare: Observe ≥ 30 min after cuff deflation for delayed LA toxicity.
Document cuff times. Check limb perfusion + neurology.
Standard procedure aftercare.

complications.management: Maintain cuff ≥ 20 min; cyclic deflation; Intralipid + ALS if it occurs.
Limit time; correct pressure; double-cuff.
Dose-limit; methylene blue if significant.
